svg.text: Services are not an architecture: an architecture is boundaries separating high-level policy from low-level detail following the Dependency Rule; services that merely
separate behaviours are little more than expensive function calls (across process or platform boundaries), architecturally significant only sometimes
TaxiUI
TaxiFinder
TaxiSelector
TaxiDispatcher
Fig 27.1: TaxiUI serves customers on mobile devices; TaxiFinder checks the TaxiSuppliers' inventories for candidates and stores them in a short-term record for the
user; TaxiSelector picks one by cost, time, luxury and so on; TaxiDispatcher orders the taxi
The Kitty problem
marketing announces kitten delivery from collection points by nearby taxis, with
only some suppliers participating, never allergic drivers, and vehicles used for
kittens in the last 3 days not offered to allergic customers: every service must
change and be deployed in coordination
Why: cross-cutting concerns
functional decompositions are very vulnerable to features that cut across all the
behaviours; every system faces this, service oriented or not; the two fallacies
(decoupling, independent development and deployment) are exposed
Objects to the rescue (Fig 27.2)
SOLID classes extended polymorphically: base classes keep the shared logic; a Rides
component holds ride-specific logic and a Kittens component the new feature,
overriding abstract bases (Template Method or Strategy), created by factories under
UI control: only TaxiUI changes and a new jar, Gem or DLL loads at runtime
Component-based services (Fig 27.3, 27.4)
give each service an internal component design so features arrive as new derived
classes in new jars on its load path (OCP); boundaries run through services,
dividing them into components that follow the Dependency Rule
